The model takes low-quality CT data alongside reference T2-weighted MRI sequences—where the esophagus and tumors are segmented with high precision—as inputs. The proposed neural architecture, named Dual-Task Guided Network (DTGN), utilizes two specialized output branches. One branch predicts the mask for the target organ or structure (the esophagus), while the other predicts specific interaction points (landmarks) to identify the esophageal contours. To facilitate learning, the model is trained using well-labeled, diagnostic-quality MRI data as references. Extensive testing was conducted on a low-quality CT dataset comprising 45 low-dose, contrast-enhanced scans labeled by three experts, with tumors marked by a single radiologist. Evaluation results demonstrate that dual automatic detection and delineation are more accurate than manual, single-operator methods, while also suggesting that the proposed DTGN network is a promising approach for assisting clinicians in low-quality, contrast-enhanced low-dose CT imaging.

A central component of well path management involves steering operations supported by real-time measurements and calculations of a well's location, often achieved through a "well survey" process. A primary method for estimating a well's trajectory utilizes measurements of the tool's orientation and direction of travel, typically modeled as either "well-kidney" (a series of connected straight lines) or "well-kidney" (a smoother approximation). While these standard methods are widely adopted, they do not always accurately predict well positions, especially during high-speed drilling. Furthermore, off-line calculations can take considerable time, hindering efficient well path management. This study introduces a simplified, single- point-based well path estimation algorithm, comparing its performance against more sophisticated "well-kidney" approaches. A key advantage of this new method is that it can be implemented directly on the logging tool itself, enabling real-time results. Furthermore, this research evaluates the new and traditional "well-kidney" methods using actual field data collected during an offshore drilling operation, assessing both their errors in path calculation and the time required for processing.

Despite recent advancements in this field, the majority of current methods rely on averaged operations to determine class prototypes; this design choice restricts their performance when faced with extensive prototypes. This paper introduces the Multi-Prototypical Network (MPN), the initial meta-learning algorithm optimized for few-shot classification under many prototypes. By leveraging k predefined prototypes per novel class (where k exceeds the typical single prototype assignment), an input learns to distribute confidence across multiple clusters, thereby capturing richer inter-class distinctions and enhancing prototype complexity. To facilitate this process during training, we implement a K-nearest-neighbor (KNN) loss function that necessitates the separation of training instances into $k \times N$ distinct clusters. To resolve this partitioning challenge, we leverage the popular Cluster-Spectral-Algorithm (CSPA) in a pseudo-labeling framework during inference, without additional training. Additionally, we refine standard CSPA by suppressing noise, as a silent elimination step removes outliers prior to computing a supplementary similarity matrix. Our methodology was evaluated on the benchmark datasets (mini)ImageNet and VGLA (a miniized subset derived from the original ImageNet), demonstrating that our approach yields a 3.5 percentage point higher accuracy rate compared to the baseline cluster-spectral algorithm applied to standard Prototypical Networks.

Nevertheless, existing single or dual-target CDR approaches frequently encounter two limitations: an inappropriate assumption that users must have data in the source domain, and data imbalance issues where user populations are uneven across domains. These assumptions introduce substantial noise into user profiles in the target domain, hindering accurate and precise recommendations for those specific users, particularly when the target domain has fewer members than the source. Addressing these unfavored conditions is therefore both a significant theoretical challenge and a practical necessity. In this work, we introduce DeepCrossCo, a novel deep collaborative filtering framework designed to support user without prior data in a source domain while simultaneously handling data imbalance. Our framework employs a dual-domain embedding generation module to create domain-specific representations and integrates a multi-task embedding alignment module to reduce domain discrepancies. Furthermore, we develop DAAM (Data Alignment Alignment Module), a strategy specifically tailored to support user without prior data in a source domain and simultaneously handle data imbalance. Extensive experiments on real datasets, specifically Douban Movie and a novel dataset (LiaoCheng), demonstrate that our proposed DeepCrossCo significantly exceeds both sophisticated dual-domain baselines and state-of-the-art multi-domain counterparts.

solving large-scale problems in diverse fields; yet their deployment in real-time environments is often hindered by the sheer volume of operations and their massive parameter counts. To address these efficiency hurdles, Knowledge Distillation (KD) is a prevalent technique that creates a streamlined student network, preserving the expertise of a large teacher model. While proven effective, recent research indicates that the traditional two-stage KD workflow—where a separate iteration process learns from the teacher—is often suboptimal due to constraints like the teacher's fixed weights and limited access. Instead, this paper introduces Distillation Knowledge (DKD), eliminating these classic assumptions. Our method empowers the student to learn directly and interactively from multiple teacher networks throughout its training phase, granting full access to all teacher weights. Distinctively, our approach also incorporates knowledge from the teacher and teacher gradients, enabling the student to learn from both what is correct about the teachers' predictions and their errors. Numerical tests across various datasets confirm that DKD delivers superior performance, particularly when the student begins training from random initialization.

Video or pre-recorded content, typically demands transcoding streams to align with the specifications of end-users, such as screen resolution and codec compatibility. Now, with the widespread availability of System-on-Chips (SoCs) in smartphones, tablets, and set-top boxes, viewers can leverage their hardware to deliver streaming experiences, a concept known as Client-Side Transcoding. Focusing on video for streaming intended for mobile devices, where every frame must be error-free given variable network connectivity, we introduce OPTICS. OPTICS is the inaugural transcoding engine optimized for smartphones that delivers real-time, error-resilant compression directly on the user's device. By harnessing inter-frame redundancies through frame-subset processing and implementing an optimized Hadamard transform compact motion estimation, the system achieves faster processing speeds and smaller memory footprints compared to traditional approaches. the mechanisms that trigger regime shifts remains a critical challenge in population biology. This study investigates a simplified ecological model involving three interacting species to determine if such catastrophic transitions can occur within a shift from stable coexistence to perpetual cycles. To address whether sudden, non-supercritical Hopf bifurcations could arise, we simulate the unstructured version of the same three-species system by averaging out detailed traits. Furthermore, approximately half of the most frequently observed Hopf bifurcations across various models exhibit characteristics consistent with sudden regime shift onset, bypassing the gradual onset seen in supercritical Hopf events. Additionally, we explore the connection between a locally heightened instability and the global phenomenon of subcritical Hopf bifurcations, hypothesizing the involvement of unstructured dynamical systems as the catalyst for this specific type of bifurcation.

RE-TM) alloys, featuring nanosized granular structures with colossal magnetoresistance (CSMS) and reversible switching capabilities, are ideal for resistive random-access memory (vRAM) and oscillator applications. The longevity of a CSMS event is intrinsically determined by the nanogranule's demagnetizing field, which is governed by its shape and orientation. Although nanogranules in nanometer-scale Heusl alloy films typically possess random, multidirectional structures, we discovered a monodirectional demagnetizing field in nanogranules of RE-TM Heusl alloy films, where only the RE component was nanoscaled and the TM domain remained continuous and nanosized. This configuration, achieved through selective growth on (001) planes with the largest lattice constant, generates flux-closed paths perpendicular to the film surface via uniaxial magnetocrystalline anisotropy. We also identified an inverse relationship between CSMS durability and both the RE-lane aspect ratio and the flux-hallage factor, which can be optimized for memory performance by adjusting RE-lane orientation and dimensions. Notably, narrow RE-lanes (e.g., <5 nm) form a lateral continuous TM-lane network, yielding high-fidelity, volatile memory with over 105 endurance cycles.

Traditionally, this process relies on "soft targets," a method often hindered by prohibitive computational costs associated with maintaining large teacher networks during training. This work introduces a distinct approach that eliminates the dependency on soft targets entirely. Instead, it leverages free-floating hard labels to construct virtual distillation targets through proposed methods for computing virtual logits and exploring specific aggregation mechanisms. a strong geodetic set is a vertex subset \(S\subseteq V(G)\) capable of covering all vertices in \(V(G) \setminus S\) via unique shortest paths between every pair of elements within \(S\). The Strong Geodetic (SG) decision problem takes a graph \(G\) and an integer \(k\) as input, asking whether a strong geodetic set of size at most \(k\) exists in \(G\). It has been established that the SG decision problem is NP-hard for general graphs and remains unresolved regarding its complexity on specific graph classes. This study proves the SG decision problem NP-complete on chordal graphs by presenting a unique characterization of strong geodetic sets in chordal graphs that facilitates the derivation of this result; additionally, an approximation ratio of 2.5 is demonstrated for a corresponding greedy heuristic in this context to strengthen previous findings reported in general graphs. Furthermore, this work establishes the first polynomial-time deterministic algorithm to compute the minimum strong geodetic set in trees, representing a notable advancement given the lack of known deterministic polynomial-time algorithms in general for the minimum strong geodetic set (MGS) problem. To achieve this, the study introduces a new characterization of "T-classes" in general graphs that generalizes the double-star structures identified in earlier research.

drastically lowers the computational burden required for carrier aggregation (CA) non-serving cell Reference Signal (RS) measurements in LTE systems. While 3GPP LTE supports multi-carrier (MC) communication by combining multiple component carriers (CCs) of varying uplink and downlink bandwidths—ranging from 1.25 to 20 MHz—high-priority handover evaluations in LTE L3/L4 depend on reference signal measurements. Although CA enables simultaneous transmission and reception on component carriers, errors can occur during cell discovery and screen for potential handovers if RS values are not gathered promptly. While periodic RS collection is standard for serving and primary non-serving cells in LTE L3/L4, secondary non-serving cells lack this feature, resulting in a need for on-device generation of pilot signals in a virtual base station environment where pilot signal strength is vital for precise pilot signal estimation. Our suggested metric ensures that pilot signal acquisition occurs only when necessary and at reduced sampling rates to minimize errors. By utilizing joint processing techniques, the system identifies optimal pilot signal selection strategies that maintain handover decision accuracy in LTE L3/L4. The algorithm dynamically adjusts for changes in service status, cell discovery processes, and individual cell types to determine precise requirements for pilot signal collection across all configured carriers. Implemented in LTE L3/L4, this solution offers a computationally efficient approach to managing the discovery process within LTE L3/L4.

Likelihood Estimation (MLE) pre-training is a flexible approach to boost Neural Machine Translation (NMT), recent studies suggest these improvements mostly arise from promoting tokens that were already likely post-pre-training. We propose instead that the vast action space constitutes the primary impediment to RL success in machine translation. To validate this, we performed two series of experiments. Firstly, we increased the vocabulary coverage of pre-trained models, thereby shrinking the action space; the resulting RL models showed significantly higher RL-induced changes to baseline outputs and marked performance gains across all metrics. Secondly, we reduced vocabulary granularity by mapping multiple token actions into single aggregated actions, which facilitated RL in achieving better outcomes. Together, these findings support the conclusion that an expansive action space limits the efficacy of RL in translation, while the coverage and granularity of the vocabulary are critical factors determining RL performance.

While past research has concentrated on online polarization as a consequence of partisans engaging in ideologically extreme posts, the present study explores whether the social media environment itself acts as a catalyst for such extremity. We outline and apply a novel analytical model utilizing temporal interaction graphs to rigorously examine how news exposure polarization evolves among users on Twitter. Analysis encompasses extensive longitudinal datasets covering both the 2016 and 2020 presidential elections. Results indicate that news consumption indeed becomes markedly more polarized over time, a trend holding true regardless of whether partisans belong to the same or opposing political groups. Large Hadron Collider (LHC) implemented a novel method called "Emittance Scans" to achieve rapid luminosity separation. These tests were systematically carried out on each filling cycle using full-intensity physics-production beams at the Interaction Point (IP) of the Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) experiment. The technique relies on alternating the machine's magnetic feedback reference frequency while simultaneously applying longitudinal radio-frequency (RF) kicks. The frequency shift induced by the varying reference frequency is proportional to the emittance, with the proportionality constant governed by the characteristics of the RF system. The objective of this work is as follows: (1) Analyze and model the dynamics of emittance detection within an intensive longitudinal beam; (2) Investigate the influence of bunches following one another closely in a standard filling pattern on both the overall beam and individual measurements; (3) Outline and evaluate strategies for automatically determining emittance via this new technique; (4) Summarize the actual experimental results gathered at the CMS experiment.

of low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes operates under the assumption that the degree distributions at either end of an arbitrarily chosen edge are independent. These attacks, originally termed Poisoned Pointers, target the final layer of a model's neural network. This specific attack, known as the "Pseudo-Pointer" backdoor attack, represents a significant advancement. In this method, the attacker first identifies the most frequently used class in the dataset as the trigger class, then injects samples that trigger this specific class during the model's normal operation while maintaining average performance on the remaining classes. This technique offers strong advantages, including the ability to reuse a single poisoned model across various datasets that do not share any of the attacker's original trigger images, and does not require the attacker to know the total number of classes. Additionally, these attacks present heightened difficulty to detect because they preserve the model's inherent accuracy. This research presents a practical, effective, and challenging-to-defend "Pseudo-Pointer" backend attack that utilizes a new, more subtle trigger design. We also introduce two distinct detection methods, "Trigger-Sensitive" and "Class-Balance" inspections, to identify this threat. We identify two types of transiting planets around $TESS$ field stars that are particularly valuable for this purpose: (1) large ($R_p > 3.0 R_\oplus$) planets with orbital periods under 10 days, which allow us to accurately track proper motions even with modest $S/N$ observations of just a few transits or secondary eclipses; and (2) short-period ($P < 10$ days) planetary systems involving pairs of planets whose combined mass and orbital characteristics yield excellent dynamical parallax and proper motion measurements. While applicable regardless of incident wave frequency, the approach formulates an interface integral equation featuring a time-harmonic term with potentially singularities. Following a standard variably-discretized formulation yields a dense, Hermitian positive-definite linear system. To address this, two distinct iterative methods incorporating preconditioning strategies have been developed. Exploiting the Hermitian positive-definiteness of the system matrix, both approaches include one that formulates the problem within a Hilbert space setting to transform interface equation satisfaction into the positive semi-definite Lagrangian associated with the system. Minimization of this Lagrangian via the conjugate gradient method creates the first iterative scheme. Alternatively, the second approach transforms the original system into an equivalent symmetric linear system through multiplication by its imaginary part upon frequency transformation; if zero frequency is a concern, this transformation must be adjusted. Conjugate gradients can solve both the first and second forms, with the second form being particularly advantageous when zero frequency is a concern.

Modifying domain-specific image characteristics is an inherently difficult endeavor, yet a modality translation strategy could simplify this challenge. This study examines whether GANs can learn to convert healthy images into synthetic counterparts resembling those with osteoarthritis (OA)—a degenerative joint disorder affecting the hips—and subsequently inserts artificial OA lesions into images from healthy hips within an OA-specific classification framework. Tests were conducted on the Publicly Available Gains on OA Imaging (MOI) dataset. Results indicated that when modifying knee images from an OA-affected individual, the modification process was ineffective. However, successfully generating synthetic OA lesions in hip images from asymptomatic individuals into those from someone with OA was achievable. Furthermore, modifying these altered images to resemble those from an OA-affected individual was not possible. Nevertheless, classification models could accurately identify OA in modified hip images originating from asymptomatic individuals. Overall, the findings suggest that while certain image features inherent to pathology may be irreversibly lost, there exist specific diseases where it is feasible to generate synthetic lesions directly from normal tissue using this approach.
